solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Silly, mardy, sad old men playing soldiers (4,4)

annotation.surface: A sulky, gloomy bunch of pensioners play at being soldiers.
annotation.walkthrough: Dad's Army is a classic British sitcom about the Home Guard, elderly volunteers defending Britain in the Second World War. Mardy is northern English slang for sulky.
annotation.definitionFit: The show's Home Guard platoon is made up largely of old men drilling as soldiers.

entries.clue: Weak-minded Democrat behind (4)

blocks.note: aft is the rear of a ship

annotation.surface: A jibe at a politician who is slow on the uptake and lagging behind.
annotation.walkthrough: "Behind" reads as lagging in the surface, but it simply supplies AFT, the nautical word for the back.
annotation.definitionFit: Daft means silly or feeble-minded.

entries.clue: Very intelligent individual with no DPhil, strangely (7)

indicatorNotes.strangely: the letters appear in a strange order

annotation.surface: A remark that a brilliant person oddly never got a doctorate.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a clever human; the individual is an animal. Dolphins are famously intelligent, and of course have no doctorates.
annotation.definitionFit: Dolphins are known as among the most intelligent animals.

entries.clue: Spy called in extremely offensive chemical weapon (5,6)

indicatorNotes.in: RANG goes in the outer letters

annotation.surface: An agent phones in about a nasty chemical weapon.
annotation.walkthrough: "Extremely" takes just the two ends of offensive, O and E, and RANG sits between them.
annotation.definitionFit: Agent Orange was the defoliant sprayed by the US military in the Vietnam War.

entries.clue: Male, lazy, nursing onset of drinker’s belly (6)

indicatorNotes.nursing: IDLE holds D as a nurse holds a baby
indicatorNotes.onset of: the start of drinker is D

annotation.surface: A lazy man is developing a beer gut.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the last word, "belly", which means the waist area.
annotation.definitionFit: A middle is a person's waist or stomach, as in middle-aged spread.

entries.clue: Fungal blight infesting farmer’s cabbage (4)

indicatorNotes.infesting: the answer lives inside the words, like a pest

annotation.surface: A disease has got into a farmer's cabbage crop.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the gap between farmer's and cabbage.
annotation.definitionFit: Scab is a fungal disease of plants such as potatoes and apples.

entries.clue: Loudly munch cutlet after eating starter of melon (5)

indicatorNotes.after eating: one word eating another takes it inside, as a mouth takes in food

blocks.note: a chop is a cut of meat

annotation.surface: A noisy diner tucks into the main course after the melon starter.
annotation.walkthrough: "Starter" is a menu word in the surface, but here it means the first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word imitates the noisy champing of jaws on food.

entries.clue: English pounds accepted by second-rate European capital (8)

indicatorNotes.accepted by: B GRADE takes E and L inside

blocks.note: L for pounds, from Latin libra

annotation.surface: A second-rate European city takes sterling.
annotation.walkthrough: B GRADE splits after its B to let EL in.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: it is one European capital among many, the seat of the Serbian government.

entries.clue: Cornish river southeast? That’s wrong (5)

blocks.note: the Fal flows through Cornwall to Falmouth

annotation.surface: Someone questions a map: is this Cornish river really in the southeast?
annotation.walkthrough: Cornwall is in the far southwest of England, so the surface's doubt is fair; the FAL is a river there.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a statement that is untrue is wrong.

entries.clue: Loot piled so high? (7)

indicatorNotes.high: high as in intoxicated, so the letters stagger

annotation.surface: A question about plunder heaped up in a tall pile.
annotation.walkthrough: "High" looks like it goes with piled, but it means drunk, which tells you to scramble the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean stripping a place of its valuables by force.

entries.clue: High-level worker wrecked Jeep’s tackle (11)

indicatorNotes.wrecked: the letters are smashed up and rebuilt

annotation.surface: A senior employee has damaged the gear in a jeep.
annotation.walkthrough: "High-level" suggests seniority, but it is literal: a steeplejack works up on church spires and chimneys.
annotation.definitionFit: A steeplejack climbs and repairs tall structures such as steeples and chimneys.

entries.clue: Very attractive, the Spanish goalie — he’s bedded plenty (11)

annotation.surface: Gossip about a handsome Spanish goalkeeper who is quite the womaniser.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface implies a seducer; a hotelier has put plenty of guests to bed in the innocent sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A hotel keeper provides beds for many guests each night.

entries.clue: Scratch word game (8)

blocks.note: the verb: to claw or scrape at something with the fingers
the board game with letter tiles

annotation.surface: A word game is called off at the last minute.
annotation.walkthrough: "Scratch" reads as cancel in the surface, but it is the verb for scraping with the hands.
annotation.definitionFit: Scrabble means to scratch or claw about, and is also the tile-based word game.

entries.clue: Cross netball player (6)

blocks.note: the football verb: to kick the ball from the wing into the middle
the netball position that plays the middle

annotation.surface: A netball player is annoyed.
annotation.walkthrough: "Cross" looks like the adjective angry, but it is the football verb: crossing or centring the ball into the box.
annotation.definitionFit: To centre the ball is to cross it; Centre is also a netball position.

entries.clue: Before stuffing down blanket (6)

indicatorNotes.stuffing: stuffing something means filling it, so one word goes inside the other

annotation.surface: Before filling a duvet with feathers, you need a cover.
annotation.walkthrough: "Down" suggests feathers in the surface, but here it means unhappy.
annotation.definitionFit: A spread is a bedspread, a cover laid over a bed.

entries.clue: Popping tablets into each drink relaxes (5,2)

indicatorNotes.into: into means going inside, so the tablets end up within the drink

blocks.note: E is ecstasy, so ES are tablets of it

annotation.surface: Someone drops pills into every drink to unwind.
annotation.walkthrough: E is slang for an ecstasy pill, so the plural ES gives tablets.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both phrases mean slackening off or letting tension go.

entries.clue: File article for newspaper (6)

blocks.note: a line of soldiers marching one behind another
a regular piece by a columnist

annotation.surface: A journalist submits a story to the paper.
annotation.walkthrough: "File" is the reporter's verb in the surface, but it is the noun for a line of people one behind another.
annotation.definitionFit: A column is a line of people in single file, and a regular newspaper feature.

entries.clue: Change for Waterloo Stn, where there’s a runaway train (5,6)

annotation.surface: Advice to change trains at Waterloo station after a train has gone out of control.
annotation.walkthrough: Alton Towers is a big English theme park, whose rides include the Runaway Mine Train roller coaster; Waterloo is a London railway station.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the theme park's Runaway Mine Train roller coaster is the train in question.

entries.clue: African city last to shut universities (5)

indicatorNotes.last to: the last of the word is its closing letter, so only that one is kept

annotation.surface: An African city is the last to close its universities.
annotation.walkthrough: "Last to shut" reads as a phrase about closing, but it just takes the last letter of shut.
annotation.definitionFit: Tunis is the capital of Tunisia in North Africa.

entries.clue: Catch sight of 40 on board heading north (4)

indicatorNotes.heading north: in a down clue, going north means reading upward

blocks.note: in darts, tops is double 20, worth 40

annotation.surface: Spotting a vessel of forty heading north.
annotation.walkthrough: "On board" hints at a ship, but it is a dartboard; tops is the double-20 segment at the top of the board.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to notice something with the eyes.

entries.clue: Bikini top reportedly outlawed? Oh … (7)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we go by how it is said

annotation.surface: Surprise that a bikini top has apparently been banned.
annotation.walkthrough: BANDEAU is French in origin and said "BAN-doh", matching banned plus oh.
annotation.definitionFit: A bandeau is a strapless band-shaped bikini top.

entries.clue: Fabulous writer regularly made a scoop (5)

indicatorNotes.regularly: at regular intervals, so the letters are taken at an even spacing, every other one

annotation.surface: A superb author has landed an exclusive story.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fabulous" means marvellous in the surface, but literally it means writing fables.
annotation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek author of fables.

entries.clue: Taking lead from smallest bridge player (4)

indicatorNotes.Taking lead from: taking something from a word removes it, and the lead is the letter in front

annotation.surface: A bridge player follows the lowest card to lead.
annotation.walkthrough: "Smallest" is LEAST, and losing its lead letter leaves EAST. In bridge the four players are named North, South, East and West.
annotation.definitionFit: East is one of the four seats at a bridge table.

entries.clue: King wearing exotic panties in disorderly house (5,3)

indicatorNotes.wearing: the K is wearing the scrambled letters around it
indicatorNotes.exotic: the letters are rearranged into something unusual

annotation.surface: A monarch in unusual underwear inside a house of ill repute.
annotation.walkthrough: "Disorderly house" suggests a brothel in the surface; here it is a place of chaos.
annotation.definitionFit: A snake pit is a scene of chaos or bitter strife.
